All Shorts

In course order.

  • Flip two fair coins. Which is more likely: two heads, or one of each?

    Two fair coins can land in 4 equally likely ways: HH, HT, TH and TT. One head and one tail happens in 2 of them (50%), two heads in only 1 (25%). Listing every outcome first, the sample space, makes the count easy; with three coins, exactly two heads is 3 of 8.

  • How many events does one die roll have?

    An event is any set of outcomes: "even" is the faces 2, 4 and 6, "a six" is just 6. Each of the 6 faces is either in an event or out of it, so a die has 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 64 events, counting "no face" and "all six". A coin, with 2 outcomes, has 4.

  • Roll a die 4 times. What is the chance of at least one six?

    Adding 1/6 for each roll gives 4/6 = 67%, but the same shortcut gives 117% for 7 rolls, which is impossible. Of the 1,296 ways to roll a die 4 times, 625 have no six at all (5 x 5 x 5 x 5), so the chance of at least one six is 1 - 625/1,296 = 51.8%. That is the complement rule: count the "none" case and subtract.

  • 10 people, and every pair shakes hands once. How many handshakes?

    Each of the 10 people shakes 9 hands, and 10 x 9 = 90, but that counts every handshake twice: once for each person in it. So there are 90 / 2 = 45 handshakes, the number of pairs you can choose from 10 when order does not matter. 23 people make 253 pairs; 100 people make 4,950.

  • 23 people in a room. What is the chance two share a birthday?

    With 365 equally likely birthdays, 23 people make 23 x 22 / 2 = 253 pairs, and any pair could match. The chance that nobody matches is 365/365 x 364/365 x ... x 343/365 = 49.3%, so the chance of a shared birthday is 50.7%. With 50 people it is 97.0%.

  • You pick door 1 of 3. The host knows where the car is and opens door 3: a goat. Switch?

    The car is behind door 1, 2 or 3, each with chance 1/3. Staying with door 1 wins only when the car was behind it (1 case of 3); in the other 2 cases the host must open the only other goat door, so switching wins 2/3 of the time. With 100 doors and 98 goats opened, switching wins 99 times in 100.

  • 5% are sick. A test catches 90% of them, flags 5% of the rest. You test positive. Sick?

    Picture 400 people: 5% are sick, so 20 are sick and 380 are healthy. The test catches 18 of the 20 sick people but also wrongly flags 19 of the 380 healthy ones, so only 18 of the 37 positives are sick: 48.6%, about half. The base rate, how common the illness is before testing, decides it: if 1% were sick the answer would be 15.4%; if 50% were sick, 94.7%.

  • 5% are sick. A test catches 90% of them and flags 5% of the rest. Positive twice. Sick?

    Picture 8,000 people: 400 are sick and 7,600 are healthy. One positive test leaves 360 sick and 380 healthy people, so only 48.6% of positives are sick; a second, independent test leaves 324 sick and 19 healthy, so 324 of 343 = 94.5%. Each updated chance, the posterior, is the starting point for the next test: a third positive would give 99.7%, still not 100%.

  • A fair coin lands heads 5 times in a row. Chance the next flip is heads?

    Six flips of a fair coin can land 64 equally likely ways, and only 2 of them start with five heads: HHHHHH and HHHHHT. One of those two ends in heads, so after five heads the next flip is heads 1 time in 2, 50%. Six heads from the start is rare (1 in 64), but the flips are independent: the coin does not remember its streak.

  • Teacher A has the higher pass rate in each section. Can teacher B be higher overall?

    In this example, teacher A passes 9 of 10 students in the easy section (90%) and 30 of 60 in the hard one (50%); teacher B passes 50 of 60 (83.3%) and 4 of 10 (40%). A is higher in both sections, yet overall B passes 54 of 70 (77.1%) and A only 39 of 70 (55.7%), because most of A's students were in the hard section. This flip is Simpson's paradox: with the same mix of students, A comes out ahead again, 70% to 61.7%.

  • Roll two dice and add them. Which total comes up most often?

    Two dice can land in 36 equally likely ways. A total of 7 comes up in 6 of them (16.7%), 10 in 3 (8.3%) and 12 in only 1 (2.8%), so 7 is the most likely total. The total is a random variable: a number worked out from each outcome.

  • Roll two dice and keep the bigger one. Which value is most likely?

    Of the 36 ways two dice can land, the bigger die is 6 in 11 of them (30.6%), 5 in 9, 4 in 7, 3 in 5, 2 in 3 and 1 in just 1. That list of chances, one for each value, is the PMF (probability mass function), and it adds up to 36/36 = 1. Keep the biggest of three dice and 6 comes up 91 times in 216 (42.1%).

  • A box has 10 eggs, each cracked with chance 10%. Most likely number of cracked eggs?

    No cracked eggs needs all 10 to stay whole: 0.9 multiplied 10 times, 34.9%. Exactly one cracked egg is 0.1 x 0.9^9 = 3.87% for any given egg, and it can be any of the 10, so 38.7%, the most likely count; two cracked eggs (45 pairs) is 19.4%. This count of yes results in 10 tries with the same chance each is the binomial.

  • A help desk averages 6 calls an hour. Which is more likely: 5 calls or 6?

    Calls that arrive at random, 6 an hour on average, follow the Poisson distribution: no calls at all has chance 0.25%, and each extra call multiplies the chance by 6 divided by the new count. The step from 5 calls to 6 is 6/6 = 1, so exactly 5 and exactly 6 calls are equally likely, 16.1% each. With an average of 4, 3 and 4 calls tie at 19.5%.

  • Roll a die until you get a six. Which number of rolls is most likely?

    A six on the very first roll has chance 1/6 = 16.7%. Stopping on roll 2 needs a miss first, 5/6 x 1/6 = 13.9%, and every extra roll multiplies the chance by 5/6 again, so 6 rolls has only 6.7%. The count of tries until the first success is the geometric distribution: 1 roll is the most likely count, even though the average is 6 rolls.

  • Prices end in random paise. Round to the nearest rupee. Average size of the error?

    Rounding to the nearest rupee moves a price by at most 50 paise: Rs 12.30 moves 30 paise, Rs 12.85 moves 15, Rs 12.50 moves the full 50. With random paise every error size from 0 to 50 is equally likely, a uniform spread, so the average size is the middle, 25 paise (20 example prices ending 00, 05, ..., 95 give 500 / 20 = 25). The signed error, up or down, averages 0.

  • Waits at a counter average 10 minutes (exponential). What share wait under 10?

    With exponential waits that average 10 minutes, the share still waiting is multiplied by 0.368 (1/e) every 10 minutes: 36.8% still wait at 10 minutes, so about 63.2% are done in less than the average. Half are done by 6.9 minutes, but a few long waits (13.5% wait over 20 minutes) pull the average up to 10. A long tail on one side like this makes a spread skewed.

  • Marks follow a bell curve: average 70, spread (SD) 8. What share score above 86?

    Measured with the standard deviation as a ruler, 86 is (86 - 70) / 8 = 2 SDs above the average. On any bell curve 95.4% of values lie within 2 SDs, so 4.6% lie outside, half on each side: about 2.3% score above 86. The same ruler gives 15.9% above 1 SD (78) and 0.13% above 3 SDs (94).

  • Can a probability density be bigger than 1?

    For a random number from 0 to 2 with every value equally likely, the density is a flat line at height 0.5, and chances are areas under it: the whole area is 2 x 0.5 = 1, and 0.5 to 1 has chance 0.5 x 0.5 = 25%. Squeeze the range to 0 to 0.5 and the height must rise to 2 to keep the area at 1. A density is chance per unit of x, so it can pass 1; the areas, which are the chances, never do.

  • A loaded die: faces 1 to 4 take slices of 0 to 1 in order. Which face gets 0.45?

    A loaded die shows faces 1 to 4 with chances 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4. Laid end to end from 0 to 1, the slices end at the running totals 0.1, 0.3, 0.6 and 1, so a random number of 0.45 lands on face 3: past 0.3 but not past 0.6. That running total of the chances is the CDF, and it is how a computer turns one random number into a roll of the die.

  • 10 people get their hats back, shuffled. On average, how many get their own?

    With 3 people there are 6 ways to hand the hats back, with 3, 1, 1, 1, 0 and 0 matches: 6 matches in 6 ways, an average of 1. Each person gets their own hat with chance 1/3, and 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 = 1; with 10 people each has chance 1/10, and 10 x 1/10 = 1. Averages add even when the events are linked: this is linearity of expectation.

  • 100 fair coin flips: win or lose Rs 100 each. How far from 0 do you typically end?

    Each flip swings Rs 100 up or down, so its squared swing is 100 x 100 = 10,000. Over 100 independent flips the squared swings add to 1,000,000, and the square root gives a typical distance of Rs 1,000 (the standard deviation), not Rs 10,000, because wins and losses partly cancel. Only 8.0% of games end at exactly 0, and 72.9% end within Rs 1,000 of it.

  • You know only a data set's mean and SD (spread). What share must lie within 2 SDs?

    The SD squared is the average squared distance from the mean, so 8 values with SD 10 have squared distances that total 8 x 100 = 800. A value 2 SDs (20) out uses 20 x 20 = 400 of that, so at most 2 of the 8, or 1 in 4, can sit that far, and at least 75% lie within 2 SDs for any data. This is Chebyshev's inequality; the 95% figure holds only for bell-shaped data.

  • A dart lands at random in a 2 x 2 square. Chance it hits the circle that fits inside?

    Every spot in the 2 x 2 square is equally likely, so each unit of area carries chance 1/4 (area 4 x 1/4 = 1). The circle that fits inside has radius 1 and area pi = 3.14, so the chance is 3.14 x 1/4 = 78.5%, and the four corners get 21.5%. The same flat joint density gives the triangle where x + y is at most 2, of area 2, a chance of 50%.

  • X is -2, -1, 0, 1 or 2, equally likely, and Y = X squared. What is their correlation?

    The five points (-2, 4), (-1, 1), (0, 0), (1, 1) and (2, 4) form a perfect U around the mean point (0, 2). Multiplying each point's x gap by its y gap gives -4, +1, 0, -1 and +4, which add to 0, so the correlation is exactly 0 even though Y is fixed by X. Correlation only measures a straight-line trend: with X = 0, 1, 2 alone it is 0.96.

  • Ice-cream sales and sunburn cases correlate (0.99). Does ice cream cause sunburn?

    In our 6-day example, ice creams sold (40 to 98) and sunburn cases (2 to 9) have a correlation of 0.99. Both follow the temperature, which rises from 25 to 40 C: it correlates 0.998 with sales and 0.995 with sunburns. A third thing that drives both is a confounder, and correlation alone cannot show what causes what.

  • Scale errors (independent): SD 3 g and SD 4 g. Add their readings: SD of the total?

    In our example each scale is off by exactly its SD, up or down, so the four equally likely total errors are +7, -1, +1 and -7. Squared they are 49, 1, 1 and 49, which average 25, so the SD of the total is the square root of 25 = 5 g, the same as 3 x 3 + 4 x 4 = 9 + 16 = 25. Variances (SDs squared) add for independent errors; SDs do not, because the errors partly cancel.

  • 20 above average on test 1. Tests correlate 0.5, same spread. Expected test 2 score?

    In our example a score is skill plus luck, each +10 or -10: skill stays, luck is new on each test, and the two count equally, so the tests correlate 0.5. Scoring +20 on test 1 takes skill +10 and luck +10; on test 2 the new luck gives +20 or 0, an average of +10 = 0.5 x 20. This is regression to the mean: expected distance on test 2 = correlation x distance on test 1, for low scores too.

  • 7 heads in 10 fair flips. After 1,000 more flips, what share of heads do you expect?

    A fair coin has no memory, so the next 1,000 flips give about 500 heads, and the expected total is 7 + 500 = 507 heads of 1,010 flips, or 50.2%. The 2 heads above half never go away, but they become a smaller and smaller share: 70% after 10 flips, 51.8% after 110, 50.2% after 1,010. This is the law of large numbers: the share settles near 50% by dilution, not by correction.
